distractorNotes: Paragraph 17 says plainly that the central question stays open, so nothing is solved at the close.
The two groups are compared, but the author never takes a side between them.
The labelling work fills two paragraphs and is described by design rather than by date.
Only paragraph 2 is historical, and the rest of the passage is not arranged by date.

answer.text: an account of a partnership, then a limit on what it shows
answer.line: Paragraphs 1 to 8 build the fungus-root trade. From paragraph 11 on, the author tests how far the sharing story can go.

steps: Split the passage into blocks before you read the choices. Paragraphs 1 to 8 build the trade: what a mycorrhiza is, and what each side pays.
Find the turn. Paragraph 11 opens "This is the point where care is required", and from there the author tests the carbon-sharing claim.
Read the close. Paragraph 17 leaves the big question open.
Match two blocks to two halves: a partnership, then a limit on what it shows.

choices.text: a problem raised in the opening and fully solved by the closing paragraph
choices.note: Paragraph 17 says what stays open: how much the carbon movement matters, and whether provisioning happens at all. The close leaves the question open.

choices.text: a comparison of two fungal groups, followed by a defence of one of them
choices.note: Paragraphs 3 and 4 do compare the two kinds of partner. But that is two paragraphs, and the author never defends one over the other.

choices.text: a series of experiments presented in the order they were carried out
choices.note: Girdling and labelled carbon do appear, but most of the passage is not experiments, and nothing is arranged by when it was run.

choices.text: a chronological history of research into the fungi of forest soils
choices.note: Only paragraph 2 is history: the 1880s and the ancient fossils. The rest is ordered by argument, not by date.
